newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights chief for quiet diplomacy in China, Cuba.
newsitem.headline: UN rights chief for quiet diplomacy in China, Cuba.

text.p: The outgoing U.N. human rights chief, defending his diplomatic approach, said on Wednesday speaking out against abuses did not always bring results when dealing with governments like Cuba and China.

Jose Ayala Lasso, criticised by human rights groups and some diplomats for his relatively low public profile, claimed his quiet diplomacy had produced results in Cuba and China where public pressure had failed.

"I'm not convinced that simply speaking out is the best way of obtaining results. We have a history of countries speaking out, U.N. institutions speaking out. I'm asking if the results obtained have been enough," Ayala Lasso told a news conference.

The former international lawyer from Ecuador, who has quit to become his country's foreign minister for the second time after nearly three years as the first U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, said he doubted if more than 35 years of U.S. embargo against Cuba had produced better human rights.

In just one visit to Cuba himself, the 64-year-old Ayala Lasso said, his diplomacy prompted the communist-ruled Caribbean island to ratify a convention against torture, free some prisoners and promote human rights.
"In the case of Cuba, we've had more than three decades of embargo and I ask: Has that produced any results?," he said.

In China, he said the proof of the success of his low-key approach was an unconditional invitation from the government for him to visit the country, accused by the West of widespread abuses. A date was never set for the visit.

"I hope the new high commissioner will be able to mix open diplomacy and dialogue with governments as I've tried to do. I hope the new high commissioner will be able to do better than I've done," Ayala Lasso said.
Not everyone is critical of Ayala Lasso. In Rwanda, diplomats say his successful deployment of more than 130 observers following 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis prevented retaliatory massacres.

In Rwanda, the U.N. human rights office had to deal with a minority Tutsi-dominated government extremely critical of the West's failure to stop the genocide and sensitive to charges of abuses by its Tutsi-dominated army.

But Ayala Lasso said he was now very worried about worsening violence in the country, where unidentified gunmen killed five U.N. human rights staffers last month. "Reports show that acts of violence are increasing in Rwanda," he said.
Throughout his term, Ayala Lasso said, his work had been hampered by lack of sufficient funding from donor countries.
Ayala Lasso had only five observers in Burundi for much of 1996 during some of the worst massacres committed by the Tutsi-dominated army.
On Zaire, he complained that his office of two observers in the capital Kinshasa was in no position to investigate recent allegations of massacres of large numbers of Hutus in the east.
"We need the political support of states transformed into practical support," he said. "How can I investigate massacres in eastern Zaire with only two people in Kinshasa?"
Ayala Lasso leaves his post on March 15.
The United Nations has appointed Ralph Zacklin, a Briton who is deputy to the U.N. under-secretary general for legal affairs, to replace him temporarily until the post is filled.

The High Commissioner for Human Rights, like the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees also based in Geneva, is elected for four years by the U.N. General Assembly on the nomination of the Secretary-General.
